en: The Scripture of King Vaiśravaṇa.

[Posthumous title: Grand Master for the Promotion of State Affairs (Kaifu Yitong Sisi), Acting Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Shi Honglu Qing), Duke of Susuo with a Fief of Three Thousand Households, Posthumously Ennobled as Minister of Works (Zeng Sikong), with the Posthumous Title "Great Mirror" (Dajian).
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra of Great Guangzhi Daxingshan Temple, acting under imperial decree.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa joined his palms before the Buddha.
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One,
for the sake of the benefit, happiness, and well-being of all sentient beings in the future,
and so that wealth and treasures may abound and the realm may be protected and maintained..."
He spoke his own mantra:
"This mantra of mine is like the cintāmaṇi-ratnarāja, capable of fulfilling all wishes."
"World-Honored One, please grant me permission to speak.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, O Heavenly King!
You are able to take pity on all sentient beings."
"Speak as you wish.
At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, filled with immeasurable joy, spoke this heart-mantra before the Buddha:
*Namo ratnatrayāya | Namo vaiśravaṇāya*.

Having spoken this mantra,
he addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One,
I shall now explain the method for receiving and maintaining the mantra."
First, take agallochum, white sandalwood, camphor, tagara, frankincense, and storax;
blend these incenses together and offer them to me, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa.
When performing the invitation, bind the root mudrā,
beckon three times toward yourself with the two index fingers,
recite the mantra seven times, and then release the mudrā over the crown of the head.

*Tadyathā | Namaḥ vaiśramaṇāya | Namaḥ dhanadāya | Dhaniniśvarāya | Accha-ccha | Aparimita-dhani-śvarā | Pramāṇikā-rūpiṇīkā | Sarvasattva-hita-cittā | Mama dhanam anuprayaccha | Svayambhuje svāhā.* The practitioner should recite this constantly and without interruption.
Finally, Vaiśravaṇa’s son, Śanisadha,
appearing in the form of a youth, spoke to the practitioner, saying:
"For what purpose do you summon my father?"
The reciter said:
"I offer this to the Triple Gem; grant me wealth and treasures.
In an instant, the youth Śakunīṣa [appeared].
Returning to the abode of King Vaiśravaṇa,
he addressed his father, the king, saying:
"The practitioner who recites this seeks all manner of wealth and treasures."
For the sake of making offerings and benefiting sentient beings,
the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa said to the youth Śanisadha:
"From this day forth until the end of your life, you shall be given one hundred gold coins every day."
That youth Śaṅkha sent one hundred gold coins every day and placed them at the head of the reciter.
Regarding those various kinds of precious coins and fragrances obtained through previous vows,
one should practice giving them away, setting aside only what is for one's own personal use.
One should not hoard or harbor stinginess;
one should constantly give rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and refrain from anger.
With superior incense, flowers, food, drink, and lamps—
In a secluded place, he made offerings to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha according to the Dharma,
while simultaneously engaging in uninterrupted contemplation for the sake of King Vaiśravaṇa and his retinue.
Out of mindfulness of his kindness and virtue, one should always recite the Auspicious Praise (*Maṅgalastotra*) so that the Heavenly King may obtain all manner of auspicious blessings.
May the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, along with his male and female offspring, retinue, and both internal and external kinsmen, provide assistance and support.
Even the messengers and their retinues, as well as all sentient beings within the borders of the kingdom, shall obtain all ten kinds of benefits praised by the Buddha. These are:
first, pure faith; [and so forth].
Second is ethical discipline;
third is learning;
fourth is relinquishment.
Fifth is feeling;
sixth is wisdom;
seventh is physical appearance.
Eighth is power;
ninth is eloquence;
tenth is mastery over form, sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, wealth, and nobility.
Within the Buddha-dharma, they opened the Dharma-eye;
they realized the fruits of sainthood and attained the sublime Dharma of the Deathless,
as well as the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that assist on the path to Buddhahood.
If the practitioner makes such a vow every day,
King Vaiśravaṇa will immediately feel great joy and announce it to his own retinue and followers:
"Observe how that practitioner has conceived deep reverence for me."
He further addressed the son Śakrāṇasa, saying:
"The practitioner who desires to behold me,
Vaiśravaṇa, the King of Yakṣas, and wishes to close the gates to the evil destinies,"
May all their sublime aspirations be fulfilled;
may they live for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of years;
and may they obtain wish-fulfilling jewels and soar through the void of space.
One will obtain *anuttara* (consecration) and hidden treasures;
men, women, and even kings will all be made to feel love and respect;
and one will also understand the languages of all birds and beasts.
May they obtain abundant wealth and be forever freed from poverty and destitution.
That practitioner of recitation should, on the eighth and fifteenth days of the waxing moon,
have an artist observe the eight precepts, bathe, and don new, clean garments.
Obtain an uncut white cotton cloth for the painting.
Do not use animal-hide glue for the pigments.
In the center, paint Śākyamuni Buddha in the posture of preaching the Dharma.
To the right of the Buddha, one should paint the form of Śrīdevī.
Her eyes are wide and long, and her countenance is serene.
Her body is adorned with a celestial crown, necklaces, and armlets.
The right hand forms the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*), and the left hand holds a blossoming lotus flower.
Having obtained the painted image,
place it in a pure location and make offerings with unguents, flower garlands, incense, food and drink, and lamps.
One should offer these to the Buddha and the goddess Śrī.
The practitioner should not give rise to fear with a base mind;
rather, they should do so with a resolute mind.
Recite this mantra of the Auspicious Goddess (Śrī-devī) according to the Dharma as follows:
*Namaḥ śrī-gaṇāya, namo vaiśramaṇāya, mahāyakṣarājāya.*
Jaya namo śrīye mahādevi tadyathā oṃ tara tara dhuru dhuru susūkṣma susūkṣma.

26. At that time, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa,
seeing one who recites this mantra and makes offerings to the Tathāgata,
took pity upon that practitioner.
Then, manifesting himself in the form of a youth or a lay devotee (*gṛhapati*),
holding a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) in his right hand and a golden casket in his left,
with a serene countenance, he approaches before the image.
Having paid homage to the Buddha image, he addressed the practitioner, saying:
"What vow do you now seek from me?
Is it to enter the cave of the asuras?"
Is it to seek hidden treasures?
Is it to seek subjugating fire or mercury?
Or is it to seek the *āṭanāṭiya* rite for winning the favor of kings?
Is there accomplishment through realgar? Is there accomplishment through the *yaśana* medicine?
Is there accomplishment as a Vidyādhara? Is there soaring through the void? Is there receiving a lifespan of one great kalpa?
Such aspirations as these shall all be fulfilled.
The reciter says to the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa:
"May I attain mastery in all places."
One attains inexhaustible wealth of gold and silver, renown, merit, and virtue;
a lifespan of immeasurable kalpas; the power to soar through the void;
and mastery over various transformations through yoga.
Vaiśravaṇa said, "I shall grant you your wish.
Then, King Vaiśravaṇa,
wishing to clarify this meaning further, spoke these verses:
Even if the sun and moon were to fall from the sky to the earth,
or the great earth itself were to overturn— such things might indeed happen,
yet one should not harbor even the slightest doubt that this Dharma cannot be easily accomplished.
Without depending on ritual fasts or purifications, one benefits those who are poor and destitute;
all people will show them respect, and until the end of their lives,
Vaiśravaṇa will provide protection, keeping them far removed from all calamities and hardships.
The yakṣa generals will provide protection, constantly following those who uphold this teaching.
If one can maintain these instructions, all wishes will be fulfilled as swiftly as a shot arrow;
kings will show reverence to such a person.
One obtains inexhaustible treasures, and ten million *koṭis* of yakṣas protect the practitioner;
one is able to fulfill all supreme aspirations,
be liberated from the evil realms, and behold Vaiśravaṇa.
Through the wealth-giving of Kuvira, one attains great wisdom and even the supernormal power of the divine eye;
one’s lifespan shall reach ten million years for those who,
with a sincere heart, cherish and revere this teaching.
One should seek accomplishment with absolute certainty and without doubt;
this method for protecting the body was taught by the deity Vighnantaka.
Through its empowerment, the supreme siddhi of mantras is attained.
Then he recited the mantra for protecting the body:
*Namo ratnatrayāya*, *namo vaiśramaṇāya*, *mahārājāya*, *tadyathā*, *oṃ*, *hūṃ*.
(The *hūṃ* is pronounced with the retroflex *ṣa*).

1. *Āḥ* (pronounced as above) 2. *Ghaṭana* (the *gha* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṭ*, as in the following) 3. *Ṭaṇṭhana* (the *ṭa* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṭ*, nasalized; the *ṇa* is pronounced with an aspirated *ṭh*, as above) 4.

*Kuṇṭha* (the *ku* is pronounced as in "district," the same as below; the *ṇṭha* is pronounced with a retroflex *ṭh*, nasalized; the syllable is in the third tone) 5. *Kuṇṭha* (the *ku* is pronounced as above) 6.
*Mahā-rāja* (the *mahā* is drawn out [protracted]) 7. *Sakṣa-sakṣa-mām* (the *sakṣa* is a conjunct of *sa* and *kṣa*; the *mām* is protracted)

(10) Now I shall explain the root mudrā.
With both hands, cross them at the palms with the right over the left;
extend the two middle fingers so their tips touch,
and bend the two index fingers like hooks.
When inviting [the deity], beckon toward yourself;
when dismissing, wave outward.
When reciting, form the mudrā at the heart and recite seven times, then release it above the crown of the head.
Thereafter, take up the rosary and recite with focused concentration.
Next, the hand-seal (mudrā) of the goddess Śrī is explained:
join the two hands together with palms hollowed out.
Extend the two index fingers, the two middle fingers, and the two ring fingers;
bend them into the shape of a lotus flower.
Extend the two thumbs and the two little fingers, joining them upright together.
When reciting, one should mentally form the mudrā and recite the mantra seven times, then scatter [the flowers] over the crown of the head.
The mantra of King Vaiśravaṇa is as follows:
*Namo vaiśravaṇāya mahārājāya svāhā. Svāhā vaiśravaṇāya ṭakki svāhā.* If one recites this over purified oil seven times and applies it to the place where one sleeps, [it will bring protection].
